READING PASSAGE 3
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 27-40, which are based on Reading Passage 3
on pages 10 and 11.
Leo Burnett
1891-1971
The advertising man who first exploited the power of the visual image
Leo Burnett, founder of the multibillion-
dollar advertising agency Leo Burmett
Worldwide, had a career spanning nearly
six decades, and an aptitude for inventing
evocative, easily recognizable corporate
identities which spawned many of the
iconic images of US commerce. As
copywriter Dalton O’Sullivan remembers
from his time working under Burnett in
the 1960s, ‘Unlike many agency heads,
Leo wasn't puffed up with his own
importance — no fancy suits, or
expectancy he should be bowed down to.
But heaven help you if you were lazy in
your approach to dealing with one of his
clients. However, if you had a well-
thought-out idea, even if he didn't like it,
he would listen —- and even change his
mind when you clicked off facts and
figures to back it up. He lived and
breathed advertising and he expected you
to do the same.
Bumett's associates recall various
techniques he used with his staff. In one,
The Group Think, a team brainstormed a
problem, a process whereby even the
wildest idea would be considered. In
another, The Creative Right Bower,
Bumett would tum to his number one
man to spark up dull campaigns and be a
constant source of grist and material for
the creative mill. Occasionally, in a move
dubbed The Outside Expert, an outsider
was brought in to evaluate a campaign.
This did not sit very well with his existing
staff, but in Burnett's defense, it must be
said that after a consultant's visit,
everyone tried a little harder. Then there
was The Creative Review Committee,
where campaigns were presented,
reviewed by all present, then reworked.
This was expensive and time-consuming,
but Burnett felt it worthwhile if it helped
them develop a better campaign.
Bumett’s advertising career began
when he joined the Homer McGee agency
in Indianapolis in 1919. Ad schemes in the
early years of the century had been based
primarily on a carefully worded argument
extolling the purported qualities of the
product being sold. Images were mere
decoration for the argument. But by 1919
product claims were giving way to
imaginary stories of consumers whose
acquisitions were rewarded with
popularity, success and romance. Burnett
moved the image to center stage. Visual
eloquence, he was convinced, was far
more persuasive and poignant than
labored narratives, verbose logic or empty
promises.
Creativity, he advised, called for an
intuitive ability to identify the ‘inherent
drama’ within a product, through the use
of down-to-earth, vernacular imagery. To
explain this, Burnett repeatedly cited a
1945 campaign for the American Meat
Institute. After careful consideration, he
related, ‘We convinced ourselves that the
image of meat should be a virile one, best
expressed in red meat.’ At the time it was
highly unusual, even distasteful, to
portray uncooked meat in advertisements.
Enthusiastically breaking the code,
Burnett produced full-page ads depicting
raw red meat against a bright-red
background. ‘Red against red was a trick,’
he explained, ‘but it was a natural thing

to do. It just intensified the red concept,
the strength, and everything else we
were trying to express.
One of the most enduring icons of
advertising history was that devised by
Burnett in a campaign for Marlboro
cigarettes. Aiming at male audiences in
the 1950s, a time when filter cigarettes
such as Marlboro were seen as appealing
mainly to women, Burmett introduced a
tough and rugged cowboy on horseback,
‘the most masculine type of man’, he
explained, to transform the image of the
brand. Other abiding Burnett creations
are the cartoon characters Tony the Tiger
and the Green Giant, icons representing,
respectively, breakfast cereal and canned
peas for generations of consumers.
Bumett admitted he rarely wrote
advertisements. ‘My greatest
contributions have been in uncovering
some basic concepts now and then,
editing, and stimulating fine talent to do
better than they ever thought they could.
Perhaps the most significant factor
contributing to Bumett’s success was this
total dedication to the creative side of the
business. As he noted, 'there's nothing
with quite the marketing leverage of the
brilliant copy idea.’ Like many other
persuasion professionals of his
generation, Burnett was obsessed with
finding visual triggers that could
effectively circumvent consumers’ critical
thought. Though an advertising message
might be rejected consciously, he
maintained that it was accepted
subliminally. Visual images evoked
responses from the ‘basic emotions and
Primitive instincts’ of consumers, he
believed. Burnett did not originate this
idea. In his classic 1922 study Public
Opinion, journalist Walter Lippmann
maintained that pictures are the surest
way of conveying a message: ‘A leader or
an interest that can make itself master of
current symbols is master of the current
situation.’ Burnett was exactly that.
Evaluating Burnett's contribution now,
in the 21" century, one is of two minds.
Created during the springtime of US
consumer culture, when sales pitches
were infused with an unfettered sense of
11
optimism, Tony the Tiger and the Green
Giant come across today as old-fashioned,
quaint throwbacks to the time when
sugared breakfast cereal, canned peas
and fat-marbled beef represented a
healthy diet. Though Burnett's corporate
talismans endure, they occupy a world
where consumers are increasingly
sceptical about the promises made about
the products offered to them. On the other
hand, the central principles that guided
Burnett's practice remain prescient. In
advertising copy, the conspicuous
triumph of typography over text, of
catchphrase over explanation, reflects
Bumett's admonition that — to the public
mind — visual form is more persuasive
than carefully reasoned argument.

According to Dalton O'Sullivan, what did Burnett require of his staff?
A support for clients’ opinions
B acceptance of his judgements
c respect for his authority
D dedication to the profession
Which of Burnett's managerial techniques motivated his staff to improve?
A The Group Think
B The Creative Right Bower
Cc The Outside Expert
D The Creative Review Committee
What was the focus of advertising before Burnett joined the industry?
A emotional appeals to the consumers most likely to buy the product
B fantasy scenarios associated with the purchase of the product
Cc graphic depictions suggesting qualities of the product
D language describing positive features of the product
Burnett’s campaign for the American Meat Institute was innovative because it
A emphasised a feature of the product seldom seen in advertising.
B used magazines then uncommon in the advertising industry.
Cc promoted a product which was not widely advertised.
D changed the public’s perception of the product.
What does the passage say about the Marlboro campaign?
A It created a symbol which has been imitated by many other
advertisers.
B It exploited a view of the product which was common during that era.
c It targeted a group of consumers not previously attracted to the brand.
D
It employed an image not previously associated with cigarette
advertising.
